source_read: PDF, Arch Pathol Lab Med 2015;139:1058-1061 (all 4 pages; text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout; pp. 1058, 1060 and 1061 (Table) checked on the rendered pages at 150 dpi; p. 1059 is figures 1-5 with captions and has no number used in the claim)

claims.overstatement: Minor: the claim's 'agranulocytosis, an almost complete loss of the neutrophil white blood cells' is stronger than this review's definition, a neutrophil count below 500 per microlitre (p. 1060); suggest 'a very low neutrophil count (below 500 per microlitre)'. The claim's 'within a few weeks' comes from the earlier review; this one says only that nearly all cases resolve once cocaine use stops, with no time frame (p. 1060). The review's own wording is causal throughout (its title calls the condition levamisole-induced; it calls levamisole the cause, and says current cases come only from adulterated cocaine because levamisole is no longer in clinical use, p. 1058); the claim rightly does not adopt it.
claims.note: Not supported by this source: the clause 'so cases were often attributed without measuring it'. The review says testing for levamisole is not required because of its high prevalence in cocaine and because the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings (p. 1060), but it gives no count of how many reported cases had levamisole measured. The next clause, 'a positive test shows exposure rather than cause', is the editors' appraisal (sound, given the ~70% prevalence the review itself reports), not the review's; the review states the opposite inference: once reports of the vasculitis appeared, researchers isolated levamisole by urine toxicology and GC-MS in patients with suspected disease, 'confirming prior suspicions that it was in fact the etiologic agent' (p. 1058, [11,12]). The claim should report that inference as the review's and label its own counterpoint as the editors'. Suggested wording: '... testing for it is not needed for diagnosis because it is so common in cocaine and the diagnosis can be made from the other findings; it also states that finding levamisole in patients' urine confirmed it as the cause, although (editors' note) since most people who use cocaine would test positive, a positive test shows exposure rather than cause.' Everything else the claim takes from this review is found and correct: about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole [3,13,14]; detected in cocaine since 2003 and detection increasing [14,15]; half-life 5.6 h, with a reference ([26], Zhu 2009), so 'a figure the earlier review does not source' is right; testing not required for diagnosis; a rising incidence asserted in the abstract (p. 1058) and an increasing incidence in the conclusion (p. 1061), with no data or citation; female predominance (male to female 1:3, mean age 44 years, both cited to a single case report, [12] Arora 2012); painful (tender) retiform or stellate purpura with or without central necrosis on the extremities, trunk, nasal tip, digits, cheeks and/or ears; leukocytoclastic vasculitis and/or fibrin thrombi in small dermal vessels, thrombi the most consistent; p- and c-ANCA, ANA, lupus anticoagulant; ideal treatment not determined, corticosteroids not shown to help, plasmapheresis only in case reports; nearly all cases resolve on stopping cocaine; surgical debridement and skin grafting after infected wounds and amputation in some reports. Screening for cocaine use by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine and m-hydroxybenzoylecgonine, confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS (p. 1060), supports 'a urine test for a cocaine metabolite'; the 1978 rheumatoid arthritis case and children treated for nephrotic syndrome support 'the same effects seen when levamisole was used as a medicine'. No rate of vasculitis among exposed people is given anywhere. Cocaine itself is not weighed as a cause: the differential diagnosis lists ANCA vasculitides, septic vasculitis, DIC, cryoglobulinaemia and warfarin or heparin reactions, not cocaine; the only mention is that antibodies to human neutrophil elastase are associated with cocaine-induced (midline destructive) lesions and may help discriminate [25] (p. 1060).

anchors.extracted: Levamisole: veterinary antihelminthic, formerly FDA-approved in humans for cancers and rheumatoid arthritis [1,2]; FDA banned its use in the US in 2000 because of adverse effects including agranulocytosis and vasculitis [3,4]; about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole [3,13,14]; detected in cocaine since 2003, detection increasing [14,15]; the vasculitis was first described in 1978 in a patient treated for rheumatoid arthritis and also in children treated for nephrotic syndrome [2,4].

Reports of a characteristic cutaneous vasculitis in people using cocaine, with neutropenia and positive ANCA, began late 2009 to early 2010 [5-10]; researchers then isolated levamisole by urine toxicology and GC-MS in patients with suspected disease, which the authors present as confirming it as the cause [11,12]; because levamisole is no longer in clinical use, current cases are said to come exclusively from people using adulterated cocaine (an assumption, not a measurement).

Predilection for women (male to female ratio 1:3), mean age at presentation 44 years [12, a single case report]; tender purpuric rash, retiform or stellate, with or without central necrosis, on the extremities, trunk, nasal tip, digits, cheeks and/or ears [7,16]; bullae, skin sloughing and bacterial superinfection [12]; ear and digit lesions reported to self-amputate [12]; leukopenia, neutropenia (including agranulocytosis), raised ESR, normal coagulation, p- and c-ANCA, ANA, lupus anticoagulant [7,11,17].

Two classic findings: leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small vessels (fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall) and multiple fibrin thrombi in small vessels of the superficial and deep dermis; often only one is present; microvascular fibrin thrombi the most consistent feature [7,12].

Thresholds: leukopenia below 4000/uL, neutropenia below 1500/uL, agranulocytosis below 500/uL; half-life of levamisole 5.6 h, detectable by GC-MS but not necessary for diagnosis [26]; cocaine use screened by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine and m-hydroxybenzoylecgonine and confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; testing for levamisole not required because of its high prevalence in cocaine and because the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings.

Ideal treatment not determined; nearly all cases resolve once cocaine use stops [7,11,12]; corticosteroids not shown to improve or speed healing [7,11,27]; plasmapheresis studied only in case reports [27]; superinfection after bullae rupture led to wound infections needing surgical debridement and skin grafting [12,27]; some reports of amputation [9,12]; neutropenia and leukopenia common.
The abstract asserts a rising and the conclusion an increasing incidence of the condition, with no data and no citation.

Differential diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitides, septic vasculitis, DIC, cryoglobulinaemia, warfarin skin necrosis, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; cocaine itself not considered; antibodies against human neutrophil elastase noted as strongly associated with cocaine-induced lesions [25]. No rate of the vasculitis among people exposed to levamisole is given.

key_findings.correction: Corticosteroids have not definitively been shown to improve or speed healing (the card drops 'definitively'); the rest (ideal treatment undetermined, nearly all cases resolve on stopping cocaine, plasmapheresis only in case reports, debridement and skin grafting after infected wounds, amputation in some reports, steroids perhaps best avoided) and the locator are confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Refs 3 (CDC 2009) and 4 (Rongioletti 1999) are cited for the 2000 ban (p. 1058); ref. 4 cannot document it, ref. 3 could. Buchanan 2012 (p. 27) does say levamisole was FDA-approved as adjuvant colon-cancer chemotherapy but not marketed for human use in the US.
Checked on the rendered p. 1059: the captions of Figures 1-5 give no source, patient or testing information.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high: agree. One domain difference for the log: I would judge the balance domain (cause and frequency) high rather than some concerns, as the Buchanan card does for the same domain. This review states levamisole as the confirmed cause (p. 1058), says current cases come exclusively from adulterated cocaine, asserts a rising incidence without data, and gives no frequency among exposed people and no consideration of cocaine itself. The overall judgment is unchanged.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: agree. Small correction to the 'claimed' text: the review does not advise against testing; it says testing for levamisole is not required, for two reasons: its high prevalence in cocaine, and that the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings (p. 1060). That cases are therefore attributed 'by assumption' is the first reader's inference (a fair one) and should be worded as the editors'.

missed: p. 1060, Laboratory findings, 1st paragraph: the second reason the review gives for not requiring levamisole testing, that the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings. Key finding 7 gives only the prevalence reason; both bear on how cases were attributed.

p. 1058, Introduction, 1st paragraph: the statement that detecting levamisole by urine toxicology and GC-MS in patients with suspected vasculitis confirmed it as the cause [11,12] appears only in the interpretation gap. Since the levamisole claim discusses how cases were confirmed, it deserves its own key finding with page and locator.

pp. 1059-1060, Pathologic features, 1st paragraph: the review says the marrow and peripheral-blood features can help tell cocaine-related from other causes of agranulocytosis [17,19]. This is another diagnostic basis for attribution, omitted from key finding 4.

p. 1058, Introduction, 1st paragraph: the review says levamisole is added for bulk and possibly to potentiate cocaine's psychotropic effects [3,13,14]. This is speculation; it is not on the card, and claims must not carry it (findings only, no potentiation language).

p. 1059, Pathologic features, 1st paragraph (continued): fibrin thrombi at different stages are said to reflect repeated insults from chronic use of adulterated cocaine [11]. This is an interpretive causal statement from one cited paper.
